content: The mean lifetime, also referred to as the average lifetime, is a quantitative measure that characterizes the rate at which a collection of elements diminishes over time, ultimately reaching zero. For an individual element within this collection, its lifetime is defined as the duration between a specified reference time and the moment it is removed from the assembly. The mean lifetime is calculated as the arithmetic average of these individual lifetimes. This concept is most commonly applied in the context of exponential decay, a specific type of decay pattern. The remainder of this explanation will focus exclusively on this exponential decay model. In the case of exponential decay, the mean lifetime (denoted as τ) of the elements in the assembly is mathematically equivalent to the reciprocal of the decay constant (λ). This value represents the time required for the population of the assembly to decrease by a factor of e (approximately 2.718). For example, Polonium-210, which has a half-life of 138 days, exhibits a mean lifetime of 200 days. The population of an exponentially decaying assembly is governed by the equation: [ N(t) = N_0 e^{-lambda t} ] Here, ( t ) represents time, ( N(t) ) is the number of elements remaining in the assembly at time ( t ), ( N_0 ) is the initial population at the reference time ( t = 0 ), and ( lambda ) is the decay constant, a parameter that characterizes the rate of decay. The mean lifetime ( tau ) is the expected value of the time it takes for an unstable element to decay. To calculate this, a normalizing factor ( c ) is introduced to convert the decay process into a probability space. Exponential decay is mathematically equivalent to a scalar multiple of the exponential distribution, which has a well-established expected value. The mean lifetime can be derived using integration by parts, confirming its relationship to the decay constant.
